name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
statement: We keep going because of what we've already spent, which we can never get back.
statementAccent: which we can never get back
meaning: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to persist in an endeavour because of resources already invested — money, time, or effort — that cannot be recovered, rather than deciding on the expected future costs and benefits. A rational chooser ignores sunk costs entirely, since they are gone whatever one does now; only what lies ahead should count. Honouring the past investment is the error captured by the phrase throwing good money after bad.
mechanism: In standard economics a sunk cost is, by definition, already incurred and unrecoverable no matter which path is taken, so it carries no information about which future action is best; only marginal, prospective costs and benefits should enter the decision. Several forces drive the fallacy anyway. One is an overgeneralised rule against waste — a wish not to appear, or feel, wasteful. Another is loss aversion: quitting reframes the prior spending as a certain loss, and people turn risk-seeking to avoid a sure loss. A third is the pull toward consistency with a decision already made.

examples.text: Sitting through a film you are not enjoying because you have already paid for the ticket — the everyday form of the error, letting an unrecoverable cost dictate how you spend the next two hours.

Britain and France kept funding the supersonic airliner partly on the grounds that so much had already been spent, lending the fallacy its other name — though historians debate how purely sunk-cost the decision really was.
Pouring more money and staff into a project that is clearly not working, to justify what has gone before — the managerial cousin known as escalation of commitment.

variants.name: Escalation of commitment
variants.text: The organisational pattern, studied by Barry Staw and others, of increasing investment in a failing course of action to justify prior investment — the sunk cost fallacy playing out over time in institutions.

variants.name: The Concorde fallacy in biology
variants.text: Dawkins and Carlisle coined the term in 1976 not to say animals commit it but to argue they should not — that parental investment ought to track future benefit, not past expenditure.

whyItMatters: It is one of the clearest and most cited departures from rational choice, with consequences from personal finance to failing megaprojects and drawn-out wars. Recognising it — learning to ask only what the future holds, and to treat what is spent as spent — is a core lesson of behavioural economics and a genuinely useful corrective in decisions large and small.

working.text: base the decision only on future costs and benefits, treating unrecoverable past investment as irrelevant to what to do now.
ask not whether the past spending will be wasted but whether the next dollar or hour is worth its expected return.
in projects and institutions, guard against pouring in more to justify what came before, the organisational form of the trap.

limits: Prescriptively the fallacy is clear, but real cases are subtler. Persisting is only fallacious when driven by past unrecoverable investment rather than by favourable expected future value; reputational and contractual consequences of quitting can make continuation genuinely rational. Whether animals show the effect is mixed and paradigm-dependent: Arkes and Ayton found no unambiguous instances in lower animals and argued children behave more normatively than adults, while a 2018 study reported sunk-cost-like sensitivity in mice, rats, and humans, but only after commitment to pursue a reward. The effect's magnitude in humans varies with framing and domain, and some reviewers argue many supposed real-world cases have rational explanations.
misreadings: Not every commitment to a long project is the fallacy — persisting is wrong only when it turns on past investment rather than future value. And the Concorde name notwithstanding, Dawkins and Carlisle did not show animals commit the error; they argued the opposite, as a normative critique of counting past investment. The cost need not be money, either: time and effort are just as much sunk.
origin: Demonstrated experimentally by Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer in 'The Psychology of Sunk Cost' (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985), with an early behavioural-economics framing by Richard Thaler in 1980; the Concorde-fallacy name comes from Dawkins and Carlisle's 1976 Nature paper on parental investment.

sources.text: Arkes & Blumer, "The psychology of sunk cost," Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35(1):124-140 (1985). — the seminal demonstration and the waste-avoidance explanation.
Dawkins & Carlisle, "Parental investment, mate desertion and a fallacy," Nature 262:131-133 (1976). — the coining of the Concorde fallacy as a normative critique.
Sweis et al., "Sensitivity to 'sunk costs' in mice, rats, and humans," Science 361(6398):178-181 (2018). — sunk-cost-like sensitivity across species after commitment.
